title: Contracts I: Formation and Interpretation
description: Analyze disputed agreements through offer, acceptance, consideration, reliance, formation defenses, writing requirements and interpretation. Four modules include original problems, a goods-and-services comparison and a complete disputed-agreement capstone.
author: Erudior
disclaimer: Independent educational preparation only; not legal advice, university credit, a J.D. degree or a determination of bar eligibility. Exercise rules are expressly simplified teaching assumptions, not the law of a particular jurisdiction. Original fictional facts and self-assessed writing exercises support introductory U.S. contracts study.

lessons.title: Identify the governing framework and a real offer
lessons.body:
A contract problem often begins with an apparently simple question: did these people agree? A useful answer must identify which exchange, which communications and which rules you mean. This lesson develops that starting method. You will separate an offer from a conversation about a possible deal and explain why the same sentence can carry different significance in different circumstances.

The course's numbered exercise rules are in the reference sheets. They supply a common starting point for practice, not a claim that every court uses identical doctrine. All named businesses and disputes in the lessons are fictional. The references link real legal texts separately. Your first task is to identify the framework before applying a remembered slogan.

## Begin with the transaction

**[[Common law]]** supplies the teaching framework for ordinary services and land transactions. **[[Article 2]]** is the sales-of-goods framework. A **[[good]]** is, for our introductory problems, a movable thing being sold. Buying printed notebooks is a goods transaction; hiring a consultant to write a communications strategy is a services transaction. A signed document is not what distinguishes them. Nor does Article 2 require both parties to be professional sellers.

A mixed transaction requires a classification argument. Under our selected **[[predominant purpose]]** test, ask what the buyer mainly sought, how the agreement describes the work, what the supplier normally does and how the price is allocated. A costly physical component is relevant but not automatically decisive. A course question may settle the classification expressly so you can focus on a later issue. In a real dispute you would verify the jurisdiction's chosen test, including whether it analyzes the transaction as a whole or particular components.

Write one sentence explaining the classification. “This is a goods problem because the exchange purchases 300 movable notebooks” does more work than “UCC applies.” It also prevents a later accidental switch into a strict common-law acceptance rule when forms contain different terms.

## Assent is evaluated in context

**[[Objective assent]]** concerns the meaning communicated through words and conduct. It does not require access to a person's private thoughts. A serious-looking signed offer may communicate commitment even if its author later says, “I was only testing the market.” Conversely, a recipient who knows the statement is a joke cannot reasonably convert it into a serious promise simply by announcing acceptance.

**[[Negotiation]]** is communication exploring a possible bargain without giving the recipient a present power to conclude it. An **[[offer]]** supplies that power: the speaker communicates a sufficiently definite commitment that the invited acceptance would finish the bargain. Ask what remains to be decided. A stated need for board approval, an unresolved scope or an explicit invitation to submit an order may show that more is needed.

An advertisement generally solicits offers because inventory, customers and final details remain unsettled. But a precise commitment to a defined performance can operate differently. Do not classify by the communication's label alone. A document titled “quote” might commit to a specific transaction, while a document titled “agreement” might expressly reserve essential approval.

### Example 1: A price email versus an offer

On Monday, Cedar Design emails a museum: “Our research packages start around 2,000 dollars. Tell us your audience and we can propose a scope.” The museum replies, “Accepted.” Apply F2 in three steps. First, Cedar has identified a starting price, not a fixed exchange. Second, its request for audience information shows that important work remains undefined. Third, the museum's reply cannot create the commitment that Cedar's email did not communicate. On these facts, the email invites further negotiation.

Change the facts: Cedar instead writes, “For 2,000 dollars we offer one audience report of 12–15 pages using the attached survey data, delivered May 20. Reply ‘yes’ by Friday at noon to accept.” Scope, price, delivery and acceptance are now specified. The invited reply would conclude the exchange. The stronger conclusion is that Cedar made an offer, even if it used “estimate” in the email subject line.

Cedar's internal note saying “hope this customer declines” does not change the communicated offer. However, if the email says “no commitment until our director signs,” the recipient must account for that reservation. Objective analysis considers communicated conditions; it does not erase them in pursuit of a bargain.

### Example 2: The booth project

Pine Studio proposes a convention project for 12,000 dollars: 10,000 for custom reusable display panels and 2,000 for layout assistance. Its usual business manufactures panels. The customer says it mainly needs physical displays and already owns its artwork. Under the course predominant-purpose rule, the tangible goods, price allocation and business context all support Article 2.

Now compare a historian hired for 12,000 dollars to research and design an exhibition, with 200 dollars of printed labels included. The customer's main objective is specialized work; the labels carry the result. The course framework points to services. Neither conclusion depends merely on whether some physical object changes hands.

Before discussing assent in either version, inspect the proposal's commitment language. If both versions require a later approval of an unresolved design, the formation question remains open. Choosing a governing framework helps identify the rules; it does not supply missing facts about agreement.

## Turn uncertainty into a useful question

A good first pass creates a short issue map: transaction, possible offer, required assent, missing terms and communications that qualify commitment. Avoid deciding the entire case from a single phrase. “We are ready” can be a commitment in one exchange and a status update in another.

Try this self-assessed exercise: a supplier says, “We can probably deliver 40 chairs at 60 dollars each, subject to warehouse confirmation.” Draft a two-sentence explanation of why an immediate “yes” may not conclude a contract. Then change one sentence of the supplier's message to make a definite offer. Compare your work with F1 and F2: your answer should discuss the reservation of confirmation and specify the performance being promised. Merely inserting “binding” without clarifying what is binding is weak drafting.

## Common mistakes

Treating a signature as the only possible evidence of assent ignores oral agreements and conduct. Treating every discussion of price as an offer ignores commitment. Treating every physical deliverable as a sale ignores the purpose of mixed transactions. Treating a hidden intention as controlling ignores what the other party reasonably understood. Each error skips a different part of the analysis.

## Key points

- Classify the transaction and explain the facts supporting that choice.
- Identify present commitment, sufficient terms and the invited response.
- Read words and conduct in their communicated context.
- State missing facts precisely instead of inventing an agreement.

lessons.title: Trace acceptance, revocation and protected offers
lessons.body:
Once you identify a possible offer, build a timeline. Who communicated what, through which method, and when did each event become legally effective? A message can be sent before another message but take effect later. This lesson uses the course's explicit timing rules to make that distinction visible. It also separates an ordinary revocable offer from an offer protected by an option or beginning performance.

## What counts as acceptance?

**[[Acceptance]]** is the invited manifestation of assent. For common-law exercises, an acceptance that insists on changing the bargain is a **[[counteroffer]]**. “I accept only if you also translate the report” rejects the proposed exchange and proposes another. “I accept; would you consider translating it for an added fee?” can be an acceptance accompanied by a request. The crucial difference is whether assent depends on the new term.

The familiar **[[mirror-image rule]]** is a starting point for common-law acceptance, not a rule that every additional word destroys agreement. Read the response as a whole. Also distinguish acceptance from a **[[mere inquiry]]**, which asks about a possibility without rejecting the offered deal. Article 2 takes a different approach to forms with additional terms; that comparison comes in Module 4.

An offer can prescribe a method or deadline. “Your signed acceptance must arrive by Friday at noon” is a receipt condition. An offer merely suggesting that email is convenient may leave other reasonable methods open. **[[Silence]]** ordinarily is not assent. Someone cannot mail an unwanted service proposal and impose payment by saying that failure to reject counts as agreement. Established dealings or knowingly accepting offered benefits can require a different analysis, but you need those facts.

## Separate sending from receipt

**[[Revocation]]** withdraws an ordinary offer before effective acceptance. Under F2 it generally works when received, not when sent. Reliable information that the offeror has acted inconsistently with the offer can also matter. Mere rumor is different from reliable notice. An offer can also lapse at its stated deadline or after a reasonable time, and other termination events may apply.

The course **[[mailbox rule]]** makes properly dispatched acceptance effective on dispatch when postal acceptance is invited for an ordinary offer. This is a limited teaching rule, not a general claim that clicking send always wins. It does not override an express receipt condition. It does not automatically govern electronic messages. For an **[[option contract]]**, the course uses receipt for acceptance. If rejection precedes acceptance, additional timing rules would be needed; our simple postal example does not silently decide that variation.

### Example 1: Crossed communications

On Monday, Mira offers a 900-dollar research project and expressly invites acceptance by ordinary post. There is no option and no receipt condition. On Tuesday at 9:00 a.m., Mira mails a revocation. At 11:00 a.m., Theo properly posts an unqualified acceptance without knowing of the revocation. Theo receives the revocation on Wednesday. Mira receives acceptance on Thursday.

First identify the effective events, not merely their dispatch order. Mira's Tuesday mailing is not yet an effective revocation. Theo's properly dispatched acceptance is effective Tuesday at 11:00 under F3. The revocation reaches Theo only on Wednesday, after formation. Therefore the course rules support a contract on Tuesday. Mira's earlier trip to the post office does not determine priority.

Change one fact: the offer says acceptance must be received to be effective. Theo's letter now takes effect Thursday, while revocation reaches Theo Wednesday. The power to accept ends first, so the same mailing sequence produces no contract through that late-arriving acceptance. A useful answer names the changed rule and effective times, not just the winner.

## A deadline is different from protection

A promise to keep an ordinary offer open until Friday may lack consideration for that promise. It may establish when the offer will lapse without making earlier revocation ineffective. An option supplies an independently supported commitment to hold the offer open. The ordinary offer and the option are related but analytically distinct bargains.

A goods **[[firm offer]]** may receive statutory protection without option consideration if its conditions are met. Save that analysis for G2: merchant status, a signed assurance, any offeree-supplied form condition and the three-month statutory limit all matter. Calling every promise to wait a firm offer loses those conditions.

### Example 2: Beginning a requested performance

An owner offers a painter 1,200 dollars “if you finish painting this fence by Sunday,” inviting only completed performance, not a return promise. On Thursday the painter buys brushes. On Friday the painter begins applying paint to the fence. The owner tries to revoke halfway through the job.

Apply F4. Buying ordinary brushes is preparation; it is not the requested fence painting. Beginning the actual painting creates temporary protection against revocation under the course unilateral-offer rule. The owner cannot revoke during the protected opportunity to complete. But starting does not automatically entitle the painter to the entire promised price: the offered payment remains conditioned on timely completion. This distinction keeps protection of the opportunity separate from satisfaction of the offer.

If the owner instead invited a promise to paint, an effective promise could form a bilateral contract before painting began. A **[[bilateral contract]]** exchanges promises; a **[[unilateral contract]]** in this teaching sense invites acceptance by completed performance. Many real offers allow either mode, so read the invitation before applying a label.

## Practice building the timeline

For each event, write four items: sender, content, delivery facts and effective time under the specified rule. Then place effective acceptance next to effective termination. If an option exists, analyze its protection before using ordinary revocation rules. If actual performance begins, identify the act that crossed the line from preparation into the invited work.

For a short writing exercise, answer: “I accept your 600-dollar editing offer if you include layout.” Then revise it into an unequivocal acceptance plus a request. Your revision should remove the conditional link. Compare “I accept the editing offer. Separately, what would layout cost?” Explain why that wording changes the commitment communicated, while recognizing that context can still matter.

## Common mistakes

Do not equate a deadline with an option, dispatch of revocation with receipt, preparation with performance, or temporary protection with completion. Do not use the postal rule for an email problem that supplies no electronic timing rule. When a problem omits a decisive fact, identify the gap and state alternative outcomes rather than choosing a convenient delivery time.

## Key points

- Read assent for conditions, requests and required methods.
- Compare legally effective events on a timeline.
- Identify option, firm-offer or performance protection separately.
- Keep beginning performance distinct from earning the promised return.

lessons.title: Find consideration and test changes to the bargain
lessons.body:
An apparent agreement is not the end of a formation analysis. Under the course bargain framework, you must also identify what each side sought in exchange. **[[Consideration]]** describes that exchange relationship. It does not simply mean that a promise was important, expensive or written down. This lesson gives you a method for distinguishing a bargain from a gift and for analyzing promises to change an existing agreement.

## Identify the requested return

A **[[bargained-for exchange]]** exists when a promise or performance is sought as the price of the other promise and is given on that basis. The return can be money, work, another promise or giving up a legal freedom. The inquiry is relational: what induced the promise and what was requested in return? A benefit arriving incidentally is not necessarily the bargained-for return.

A **[[legal detriment]]** means surrendering a legal freedom or undertaking an obligation; it does not require physical injury or a bad financial deal. A person can supply consideration by promising not to enter a permitted competition. Conversely, performing a duty already owed to the same promisor ordinarily supplies no new consideration for a later promise to pay extra.

Distinguish economic **[[adequacy]]** from the existence of an actual exchange. Courts generally do not reprice a genuine bargain simply because one party obtained a better deal. A sham dollar recital is different: if neither side intends the dollar to be exchanged, the recital may not establish the bargain claimed. Other doctrines can still address unfairness, incapacity or deception even when consideration exists.

### Example 1: A discount and a gift condition

Nora owns a used drafting table. She offers to sell it to a student for 15 dollars although similar tables sell for 200. The student promises to pay and Nora promises to transfer it. First identify the exchange: the table is promised for the student's payment, and payment is promised for the table. Second, separate price inequality from absence of exchange. A deliberately generous price does not itself eliminate consideration. Third, leave any independent defense to its own analysis; none is supplied here.

Compare Nora's message, “I am giving you the table. Come to my garage to collect it.” Walking to the garage may cost time, but the facts suggest a **[[conditional gift]]**: collection is a practical condition of receiving the gift, not a service Nora seeks to buy. Change the message to “I will give you the table if you catalog my tools for two hours,” and the requested work supplies a different exchange. The same physical table can be the subject of a bargain or a gift depending on the communicated relationship.

To test the distinction, ask why the promisor requested the act. That question is not a search for hidden motive; it is an interpretation of the promise and circumstances. Avoid making every inconvenient condition into consideration simply because the recipient expends effort.

## Time and discretion can defeat the proposed exchange

**[[Past consideration]]** is a misleading label for an act completed before the promise and not bargained for in exchange for it. Suppose a neighbor voluntarily retrieves a lost bicycle. The owner later promises 100 dollars in gratitude. The earlier rescue did not occur in exchange for that later promise. Under F5 the ordinary bargain theory is missing, though specially supplied exceptions could change a different problem.

An **[[illusory promise]]** leaves performance entirely optional, so it supplies no meaningful commitment. “I will buy as many as I decide, including none for any reason” may reserve complete discretion. A genuine requirements arrangement is different if it commits the buyer's actual good-faith needs to the seller. The word “requirements” is not enough by itself; identify the restriction on discretion. Good faith and the relevant sales rules do work that an unlimited escape clause does not.

A settlement of a disputed claim can also present consideration questions, but the validity of forbearance depends on the applicable standards for the claim and the parties' beliefs. Do not assume every threat to sue is valuable consideration. These lessons flag that boundary without inventing a universal settlement rule.

### Example 2: An extra payment for unchanged work

A translator has already agreed to translate ten pages for 500 dollars by Friday. On Wednesday, without any new circumstance, the translator says, “Pay 100 more or I will not finish.” The client agrees. The translator undertakes no extra work. Under the course **[[preexisting duty]]** rule, completing the same ten pages supplies no fresh consideration for the added payment. A bare new signature does not itself solve that problem.

Now the client requests five additional pages, and the translator promises all fifteen for 750 dollars. The added five pages are a new obligation and can support the changed bargain. You should specify that obligation rather than write only “there is new consideration.” A genuinely new duty changes the exchange analysis.

Finally, suppose an unforeseen technical problem dramatically increases the work and both parties fairly adjust the arrangement. Some common-law approaches recognize modifications based on unanticipated circumstances. F6 identifies that exception as a research issue; unless the exercise supplies its conditions, do not declare the modification either universally valid or universally invalid. A basic classroom rule is an analytical starting point, not an excuse to suppress known qualifications.

## Compare goods modifications carefully

A **[[modification]]** changes an existing agreement. Under Article 2, new consideration is not required, but that does not make every demanded change enforceable. Good faith remains important, as do writing requirements and valid signed-modification clauses. A manufacturer who threatens to withhold goods merely to exploit the buyer's emergency cannot rely on “no consideration required” as a complete answer.

Keep two questions separate: did the parties assent to a change, and is that change enforceable under the applicable framework? A unilateral invoice stating a higher price does not automatically establish assent. Similarly, the original agreement does not disappear merely because an attempted modification fails. Later waiver and performance consequences belong mainly to Contracts II.

## Write the exchange in two arrows

For a self-check, put the first promise in one sentence and the requested return in another. Then identify any existing duty, completed past act or unrestricted discretion. This small discipline prevents vague conclusions such as “both benefit.” Explain whether each claimed return was actually requested as part of this bargain.

## Common mistakes

Do not confuse a useful act with a bargained-for act, a low price with no consideration, a new signature with a new obligation, or Article 2's modification rule with permission for coercion. Do not use reliance as an invisible substitute for missing consideration; give that separate theory its own elements in the next lesson.

## Key points

- Name the promise and the requested return.
- Examine timing, existing duties and genuine limits on discretion.
- Separate consideration from adequacy and independent defenses.
- Apply the correct modification framework and preserve its qualifications.

lessons.title: Analyze reliance without inventing a bargain
lessons.body:
Sometimes a promise causes a serious change of position without a bargained-for exchange. It is tempting either to enforce every such promise or to dismiss every loss once consideration is missing. **[[Promissory estoppel]]** supplies a more disciplined alternative. The course F7 rule requires a promise, foreseeable and reasonable detrimental reliance caused by it, and a need for enforcement to avoid injustice. This lesson teaches the links, the counterarguments and the limits of that analysis.

## Start with what was actually promised

A **[[promise]]** communicates commitment to act or refrain from acting in a specified way. “We are interested in working with you” can encourage hope without committing to hire. “We will reimburse the nonrefundable room deposit up to 300 dollars if approval falls through” is a much more definite undertaking. Identify the specific commitment being enforced before discussing the claimant's expenses.

Foreseeability asks whether the promisor should reasonably anticipate the kind of action taken. **[[Reliance]]** asks what the claimant actually did or refrained from doing because of the promise. **[[Causation]]** connects them: an expense already incurred before the promise cannot have been induced by it. An expense incurred afterward may still have an independent cause. Sequence is necessary evidence, not a complete explanation.

**[[Reasonable reliance]]** evaluates the decision in context. Express warnings, unresolved approvals and limits on reimbursement can matter. A promise to cover one room deposit does not invite unlimited expansion of a project. Keep the claimant's strongest argument and the promisor's strongest response visible. A reasoned conclusion can recognize both without treating every uncertainty as a tie.

### Example 1: The promised deposit protection

A workshop organizer tells a speaker, “The full workshop still needs board approval, but reserve the room today. If the board declines, we will reimburse your nonrefundable deposit up to 300 dollars.” The speaker would not otherwise reserve the room and pays a nonrefundable 240-dollar deposit that day. The board later declines.

First separate two proposed commitments. There may be no final workshop contract because approval remains outstanding. But the organizer made a distinct and specific reimbursement promise. Second, the organizer expressly requested the reservation, so that expenditure was foreseeable. Third, the speaker's statement and payment record connect the promise to an actual loss. Fourth, staying within the stated cap supports reasonableness. Fifth, nonrefundability and the absence of another recovery support an injustice argument. These facts give the reliance theory substantial support under F7.

Do not leap to the workshop's entire anticipated speaking fee. The promise concerned deposit protection, and relief under F7 may be limited as justice requires. Also examine bargain theory separately: if the reservation itself was sought in exchange for reimbursement, a court could view it as consideration. Alternative theories are acceptable when their requirements are analyzed distinctly. A claimant should not obtain duplicative recovery merely by naming two theories.

## Organize evidence by element

A practical reliance table contains the promise's exact wording, the action claimed, its date, why it was taken, why it was reasonable and what loss remains. Refunds, reusable purchases and alternative opportunities affect the loss assessment. They do not erase the original communication, but they may change what enforcement is needed to avoid injustice.

**[[Forbearance]]** is refraining from an action. Turning down a definite competing engagement may be a change of position, but a vague claim that “other opportunities existed” is weaker than a dated offer declined because of the promise. Ask what the claimant could have done without the promise and what reliable evidence supports that counterfactual. Avoid inventing profitable work that was never actually available.

A **[[reliance remedy]]** aims to address the justified change of position within the governing doctrine; its scope is not automatically identical to the benefit of the proposed bargain. This course introduces that limit without teaching a universal damages formula. Detailed remedy rules, mitigation and offsets belong in Contracts II and jurisdiction-specific research.

### Example 2: Enthusiasm and an earlier expense

Before meeting a potential client, a designer buys a 700-dollar drawing tablet for use across many projects. At the meeting, the client says, “Your ideas are promising; send a proposal for the board to consider.” Hoping to secure the work, the designer later pays 100 dollars to make an optional presentation booklet without telling the client. The board chooses someone else.

Analyze the tablet first. It predates the statement, so the statement did not cause its purchase. The tablet's continued usefulness further complicates any claim of loss, but causation already fails. Analyze the booklet separately. It followed the statement, yet the statement expresses interest and requests a proposal rather than promising a contract or reimbursement. The proposal process itself signaled uncertainty. The designer's disappointment does not supply the missing promise.

A changed fact could matter: if the client expressly promised to reimburse necessary proposal-printing costs and requested the booklet, there would be a different undertaking to analyze. Strong legal reasoning identifies that distinction instead of declaring that precontractual expenses are always recoverable or never recoverable.

## Keep neighboring theories distinct

**[[Restitution]]** focuses on an unjustly retained benefit, rather than simply enforcing a promise or reimbursing every expense. A person can spend money without conferring a benefit on the defendant. Conversely, a benefit issue can arise without an enforceable promise. This course uses restitution as a boundary marker; it does not supply every element or defense for a restitution claim.

A writing requirement can also complicate reliance. F7 does not automatically override the statute of frauds. If a land agreement lacks the required writing, you need the governing rule on exceptions and estoppel. It is not enough to show that the claimant acted sincerely. Module 3 teaches the writing screen and the importance of a rule for each claimed exception.

## Your turn: a short alternative analysis

Using the reimbursement facts in Example 1, write one paragraph on possible consideration and one on promissory estoppel. In each, state the distinct rule and connect it to the reservation. End with the factual information you would verify: exact wording, authority, payment, refundability and the reason for booking. Your answer should preserve the board-approval condition for the larger workshop while recognizing the narrower promise.

## Common mistakes

Avoid replacing a promise with optimism, treating every later expense as caused by the promise, ignoring refunds, or awarding the entire hoped-for contract value. Do not disguise a reliance argument as consideration simply because money was spent.

## Key points

- Identify the precise commitment before listing losses.
- Prove foreseeability, actual action, causation and reasonableness separately.
- Explain why enforcement is needed and what limits may apply.
- Keep bargain, reliance and restitution theories analytically distinct.

lessons.title: Evaluate capacity, pressured consent and mistake
lessons.body:
A person can appear to accept a bargain that has consideration yet possess a defense to enforcement. The facts supporting assent do not answer every question about how that assent was obtained. This lesson introduces a structured defense screen: capacity, false assertions, improper pressure, mistake, unfairness and illegality. Use the course D rules for the exercises, and identify where a real dispute would require additional law.

## Use the consequence precisely

A **[[voidable]]** agreement can operate unless the protected party takes the steps needed to avoid it. A **[[void]]** agreement has no legal effect in the relevant sense. An **[[unenforceable]]** agreement faces a barrier to judicial enforcement. These terms are not interchangeable, and a single slogan rarely states every consequence. Ask who can assert the defense, what facts trigger it and what follows if it succeeds.

**[[Capacity]]** concerns a person's legal ability to undertake the transaction. Under D1 an ordinary minor's contract is generally voidable at the minor's election, subject to exceptions. It is inaccurate to say that every agreement involving a minor never existed. Necessaries, ratification after majority and duties to restore benefits can matter. A mental-health diagnosis also does not automatically establish incapacity; the applicable functional test and circumstances of the transaction matter.

## Identify the defect in consent

**[[Misrepresentation]]** concerns a qualifying false assertion that induces assent through justified reliance. Under D2 a fraudulent or material assertion can support avoidance. Intentional deception is powerful evidence, but materiality and fraud are not identical concepts. A sincere but materially false assertion may raise an avoidance issue under the course rule. Conversely, a lie that did not induce the deal does not satisfy every required element.

**[[Duress]]** requires more than a hard bargain or urgent need. Identify the improper threat, its causal role and the absence of a reasonable alternative. **[[Undue influence]]** focuses on unfair persuasion connected to vulnerability or domination. A trusting relationship supplies context, not an automatic defense. The analysis should explain how the relationship was exploited in obtaining this assent.

### Example 1: A false inspection statement

An equipment seller tells a small bakery, “This mixer passed yesterday's required safety inspection.” The inspection actually failed. The seller knows the result and speaks to induce a sale. The bakery asks specifically about certification, reasonably relies on the answer and purchases the mixer because it needs equipment approved for immediate use.

Begin with the assertion: a statement about an actual inspection result is a factual claim, not merely praise. The failed report makes it false, and knowledge supports fraud. Next connect it to assent: the bakery's question and stated need explain why the representation induced the purchase. Finally consider justified reliance under the stated facts. The course D2 elements support a substantial avoidance argument.

Change the facts so the bakery already read the failed report and bought the mixer solely for spare parts. The seller's lie remains troubling, but this buyer did not rely on it in entering the transaction. The defense described requires that missing link. This variation teaches why moral disapproval is not a substitute for applying each legal element. Other claims or regulations might apply, but they require their own rules.

Now imagine the seller simply omitted the report without making a statement. Nondisclosure can matter under appropriate duties and circumstances, but D2 does not make all silence fraudulent. Identify a disclosure duty, a misleading half-truth or another supplied basis before reaching the same conclusion.

## Distinguish mistake from an unwanted future

A **[[mutual mistake]]** concerns a shared erroneous belief at formation about a basic assumption, materially affecting the exchange. The risk of that error matters. **[[Risk allocation]]** can appear in express language or in a party's conscious decision to proceed with limited knowledge. A disappointing future development is different from an erroneous existing fact.

A **[[unilateral mistake]]** affects only one party and generally needs additional conditions for relief. The course does not make every spreadsheet error an escape from a contract. Ask whether the other party knew, whether enforcement would meet the relevant unfairness standard and who assumed the risk under the governing law. Without a supplied rule, identify those questions rather than invent the result.

### Example 2: The sealed equipment crate

A seller and buyer both believe a sealed crate contains a functioning laboratory pump. They contract on that shared understanding. In fact, before formation, an unnoticed fire destroyed the pump inside. The pump's existence is basic to the exchange, and its destruction materially changes what the buyer receives. If the buyer did not assume this risk, D3 supports a mutual-mistake avoidance argument.

Change the document: it expressly sells “unknown salvage contents; buyer accepts the risk that no usable pump remains.” Both parties know the contents are unverified. The buyer cannot simply repeat “we were wrong” while ignoring the allocation of uncertainty. The agreement may assign the very risk that occurred. You must analyze that language and the circumstances before treating the mistake as a basis for avoidance.

Change the facts again: the pump exists and works at formation, but market prices fall afterward. That is ordinarily a changed circumstance or failed forecast, not the same erroneous existing fact. Separate a formation mistake from later developments; Contracts II addresses additional doctrines concerning performance and changed conditions.

## Screen unfair terms without collapsing the analysis

**[[Unconscionability]]** examines serious defects in process and excessively one-sided terms under the selected framework. Hidden terms, lack of meaningful choice and extreme allocation of burdens may matter. A standard form or a high price alone does not establish every requirement. The balance between procedural and substantive concerns and the available remedies varies by jurisdiction.

**[[Illegality]]** and public policy can also prevent enforcement, but the analysis needs an actual prohibition or identifiable policy. An agreement to commit a prohibited act differs from a lawful transaction that merely feels unfair. Do not label every disliked clause void without identifying the source and scope of the limitation.

## A defense worksheet

For each plausible defense, write the triggering fact, the missing element, the strongest response and the possible consequence. In the mixer example, the failed inspection report supplies falsity; the purchase decision supplies reliance. In the crate example, the risk clause supplies the principal response. This method makes your writing useful even when the conclusion is conditional.

## Common mistakes

Do not equate pressure with duress, diagnosis with incapacity, a price decline with mutual mistake, or a lie with proven reliance. Do not omit risk allocation. Do not promise automatic cancellation when avoidance, restoration and affirmation rules remain to be researched.

## Key points

- Analyze defenses after identifying the apparent bargain.
- Tie each element to a concrete fact and a counterargument.
- Distinguish existing error from future risk.
- State the possible legal consequence precisely and preserve unresolved conditions.

lessons.title: Apply writing requirements and their limited exceptions
lessons.body:
An oral agreement can exist even when a legal rule limits its enforcement without a signed record. The **[[statute of frauds]]** is a family of writing requirements for particular categories of transactions. It is not a universal command that every contract be written, and its name does not mean the claimant must prove fraud. This lesson separates formation from the writing screen and teaches how exceptions work without swallowing the rule.

## Ask four questions in order

First, what category triggers a writing requirement? Second, what information and signature does the applicable rule require? Third, do the actual records satisfy it? Fourth, if not, does a specified exception apply, and how far? The **[[party to be charged]]** is the party against whom enforcement is sought. A record signed only by the claimant may not satisfy a requirement for the other party's signature.

For D4 common-law exercises, land transfers and agreements incapable of full performance within one year of making receive a writing screen. These are selected categories, not a complete statutory list. A **[[memorandum]]** can record the essential bargain without being an elaborate formal contract. Multiple documents, agent signatures and incorporation can raise additional questions; do not assume facts or rules the problem does not supply.

The **[[one-year rule]]** measures from making the agreement. Expected duration and possible completion are distinct. An indefinite assignment that might finish in eight months is not necessarily within the rule merely because everyone expects two years. Conversely, a fixed eighteen-month service obligation cannot be fully performed within one year simply because a party might breach it tomorrow. A termination option also requires careful treatment; termination is not automatically full performance.

### Example 1: The start date changes the clock

On January 1, a consultant orally promises to provide continuous services from March 1 through the following February 28, with no shorter completion contemplated. Performance lasts about a year, but the bargain is made two months before it begins. Under D4, full performance extends beyond one year from formation. The relevant clock does not restart on March 1.

Now change the promise to prepare a report whenever completed, with an estimate of fourteen months but no minimum duration or term preventing earlier completion. If completion within a year is possible under the agreement, the expected fourteen months alone does not satisfy the course one-year category. Explain that conclusion through the promise's terms, not a prediction that this consultant probably works quickly.

Neither version decides whether some other statute requires writing or whether a recognized exception applies. For example, full-performance exceptions require their own rule. The course does not silently use part performance to cure every services agreement. A disciplined answer can complete the selected screen while identifying a question beyond its scope.

## Goods have a distinct writing rule

Under D5, a sale of goods for at least 500 dollars generally requires a signed writing indicating a contract and stating quantity. The 500-dollar amount is the course's selected Article 2 threshold, not a promise that every jurisdiction and transaction uses that figure forever. The **[[quantity term]]** limits enforcement through the writing. Missing or misstated details do not always defeat it, but a writing for ten units does not by itself prove an enforceable promise for a hundred.

Electronic messages can supply relevant records. An **[[electronic signature]]** requires more analysis than seeing a typed name: attribution and intent to adopt the record matter, along with the applicable law. For course problems that expressly stipulate those requirements, use the typed signature accordingly. Federal electronic-form protections preserve other substantive requirements; they do not manufacture assent or fill in a missing quantity.

### Example 2: A merchant confirmation and a disputed quantity

Two merchants discuss a sale of 80 chairs for 4,800 dollars. The seller promptly sends a signed confirmation accurately describing an alleged 80-chair bargain. The buyer receives it, has reason to know its contents and makes no written objection within ten days. Assume the confirmation is sufficient against its sender and all D5 timing conditions are met.

The **[[merchant confirmation]]** route can satisfy the writing requirement against the recipient even without that recipient's signature. But this conclusion does not prove that the oral bargain happened. If the buyer credibly disputes whether agreement was reached or says only 50 chairs were discussed, those formation and quantity issues remain. The exception addresses the writing barrier, not every disputed fact.

Change the facts: the buyer timely objects in writing to the confirmation. That prevents use of this particular no-objection route. It does not automatically disprove an existing agreement or prevent proof through a different sufficient record or exception. Avoid treating the ten-day provision as either a universal acceptance rule or an automatic cancellation right.

## Apply exceptions to their actual extent

**[[Specially manufactured goods]]** can qualify when they are unsuitable for ordinary resale and the seller makes a substantial beginning or procurement commitment before receiving repudiation, in circumstances indicating they are for this buyer. An unstarted plan to customize ordinary inventory does not necessarily meet the exception. Identify the work and its timing.

An **[[in-court admission]]** can support enforcement to the quantity admitted under D5. A casual private message is not automatically that exception, though it may have other evidentiary or writing significance. **[[Receipt and acceptance]]** of goods can support another path for those goods. Delivery alone and acceptance are different facts. Payment made and accepted also has a limited statutory role; partial payment is not a universal solution for an entire disputed quantity.

Suppose an oral deal concerns 30 mugs and the buyer receives and accepts six. Under the specified acceptance exception, those six have a supported path around the writing barrier. The other 24 require another basis. Do not infer that acceptance of a sample necessarily validates every claimed unit. The limiting words are part of the rule, not optional fine print.

## Connect this screen to the capstone

The Harbor Workshop record includes a signed goods order specifying 200 notebooks and expressly stipulates electronic attribution. Identify who signed and against whom enforcement is sought. Then distinguish that record from the separate services exchange, which has its own approval and timing facts. Treating all communications as one undifferentiated “contract” would obscure both analyses.

## Common mistakes

Avoid saying oral equals void, expected duration equals required duration, electronic equals invalid, or silence after a confirmation proves agreement. Do not describe an exception without its quantity, timing or manufacturing limits. Do not assume reliance overrides the writing rule without authority.

## Key points

- Separate agreement from enforceability through a writing.
- Identify category, required content, signature and exception.
- Measure the one-year screen from formation.
- Preserve the limits of each goods exception.

lessons.title: Interpret the agreement and evaluate earlier statements
lessons.body:
After asking whether an agreement exists, ask what it means. A contract can be sufficiently definite to form yet leave room for disagreement about a phrase. This lesson develops an interpretation method and distinguishes it from adding an earlier promise to a final writing. You will also learn why a signed contract does not automatically make every surrounding communication irrelevant.

## Identify the competing readings

**[[Interpretation]]** determines the meaning of the agreement. Begin with the actual words, then read the document as a whole and identify permissible context. A strong analysis states each plausible reading before choosing between them. **[[Ambiguity]]** is a meaningful uncertainty between reasonable readings, not merely the fact that two people disagree. A strained private meaning does not become reasonable because one party insists on it.

The course I1 rule asks what the parties communicated and had reason to understand. If they attach materially different reasonable meanings and neither knows or has reason to know the other's meaning, the problem may be a failure of agreement on that term. If one side knows the other's meaning while the other is unaware of the divergence, the analysis changes. Do not use a slogan about “meeting of minds” instead of those facts.

Context can include the transaction's purpose and recognized practices, subject to the governing rules. Different jurisdictions use different approaches to when outside context may be considered. In these exercises use I1–I3; in actual research identify the forum's method before importing every negotiation into the interpretation.

### Example 1: What does delivery mean?

A signed order requires “delivery to the workshop by June 14.” Elsewhere it provides the workshop's street address and says the notebooks will be handed out there June 15. The seller argues that tendering boxes to a carrier on June 14 satisfies delivery. The buyer argues the goods must reach the workshop by that date.

Start with the preposition and destination: “to the workshop” supports arrival at that place. Read the event date and address alongside that phrase; they strengthen the buyer's explanation of why arrival matters. The seller needs a textual or contextual basis for treating dispatch as delivery. A general claim that “we always ship this way” does not establish a shared contractual meaning without evidence of an applicable practice or agreement.

Now change the signed language to “shipment by June 14” and specify that carrier transit is outside the seller's control. The interpretation changes because the agreed wording changes. Do not force the buyer's event deadline into a document that communicates a different allocation. A sympathetic purpose is relevant context, not permission to rewrite clear terms.

## Distinguish finality from completeness

An **[[integration]]** is a writing adopted as final for the terms it contains. A **[[partial integration]]** can be final without containing every term. A **[[complete integration]]** is intended as the complete and exclusive statement within its scope. The **[[parol evidence rule]]** addresses using certain earlier or contemporaneous agreements to contradict or supplement a final writing. Despite its name, it is not limited to spoken evidence; an earlier email can present the same issue.

Under I2, a final writing cannot be contradicted by a prior or contemporaneous inconsistent term. A partial integration may permit a consistent additional term. A complete integration also excludes consistent additions within its scope. First identify what the offered evidence is meant to prove. Explaining the meaning of a phrase, challenging validity and asserting a later modification are distinct tasks from adding an earlier inconsistent bargain.

An **[[integration clause]]** is evidence that the parties intended finality or completeness. It does not automatically erase fraud, eliminate every interpretive issue or prevent every later change. Its legal effect depends on the applicable doctrine and circumstances. Do not treat the clause as a shortcut around identifying the purpose and timing of evidence.

### Example 2: Earlier price and later change

A consulting agreement signed on April 5 states a final fee of 3,000 dollars and is stipulated to be a complete integration of the project terms. One party offers an April 2 email promising a 2,500-dollar fee to prove that the contract price is lower. Under I2 that use contradicts the final price term. The earlier email does not control merely because it is written.

Next, the same party offers an April 8 email in which both sides agree to add a new workshop for an additional 400 dollars. That is a proposed later modification. The parol evidence rule does not exclude it simply because the April 5 document was complete when signed. Whether the change is effective requires assent, consideration or the applicable modification rule, plus any formalities. Different legal questions govern different uses of evidence.

Finally, suppose the April 2 message is offered to show that a signature was procured through a material deception, rather than to replace the price term directly. That raises a validity issue. The integration label alone does not resolve it under our course framework. You must analyze the relevant defense and any jurisdictional qualifications.

## Goods context has named categories

**[[Course of performance]]** concerns repeated conduct under this agreement, with the necessary knowledge and opportunity to object. **[[Course of dealing]]** concerns earlier transactions between the same parties. **[[Usage of trade]]** concerns a sufficiently established practice in the relevant trade. These categories supply different evidentiary relationships; they are not three names for whatever the seller usually does.

Under I3, try to harmonize express terms and qualifying context. If they cannot reasonably be reconciled under the selected hierarchy, express terms outrank performance, performance outranks dealing, and dealing outranks usage. Waiver and notice questions can complicate application. A novice answer often jumps straight to a hierarchy without first asking whether the evidence really qualifies or conflicts.

For example, three prior notebook orders packed 25 to a carton may help explain an unstated packing practice as course of dealing. But that history does not automatically override an express current term requiring cartons of 20. If the buyer knowingly accepts a different packing practice repeatedly under the current agreement, performance or waiver issues may arise; label the facts accurately before deciding their effect.

## Write a balanced interpretation paragraph

Use the Harbor record's “delivery to Harbor” clause. State the arrival reading, the supporting text and the seller's best available response. Explain why an earlier dispatch discussion may have limited force against a later specific destination term. Then identify the exact missing fact that would matter, such as whether the signed language was actually adopted as final. The record stipulates that point for this exercise, so do not manufacture uncertainty where it has been resolved.

## Common mistakes

Do not equate disagreement with ambiguity, a signature with complete integration, parol with oral only, or a later modification with an earlier inconsistent promise. Do not use a trade practice without evidence that it qualifies. State the function of every proposed contextual fact.

## Key points

- Compare plausible meanings using text and permitted context.
- Determine finality and completeness separately.
- Classify evidence by timing and purpose.
- Distinguish performance, dealing and trade usage before applying priority rules.

lessons.title: Compare sales formation and write the disputed-agreement analysis
lessons.body:
This final lesson brings the course together. Article 2 can recognize agreement despite open terms or conflicting forms, but it does not make every proposed term binding. You will separate the existence of a goods contract from its contents, then analyze the Harbor Workshop record across formation, reliance, enforceability and interpretation. The goal is an organized explanation with factual support and calibrated conclusions.

Allow about two hours for this lesson, including drafting the capstone and checking it against the rubric. The writing is self-assessed.

## Agreement can be broader than matching forms

Under G1, a sale can be established through words or conduct without identifying a single perfect moment of formation. **[[Open terms]]** do not necessarily defeat agreement when the parties intend to contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for a remedy. That flexibility is not permission to invent any quantity, scope or price the analyst prefers. State what the parties actually committed to and which supplied rules fill a gap.

A goods offer ordinarily invites a reasonable method of acceptance unless the language or circumstances unambiguously require otherwise. For a prompt-shipment order, a prompt promise to ship or actual shipment can accept. A **[[nonconforming shipment]]** may both accept and breach. An **[[accommodation]]** is a differently framed response: with seasonable notice that the shipment is offered only as an accommodation, that shipment does not accept under G3. The buyer's later response then matters. Calling everything shipped an acceptance loses the statutory qualification.

### Example 1: Substitute folders

A school orders 50 blue folders for prompt shipment. The seller promptly ships 50 green folders without explanation. Under the stipulated G3 rule, shipment can accept the order while breaching its color requirement. Formation and proper performance are separate inquiries; a contract is not necessarily absent simply because the goods are wrong.

Change the seller's response: before shipment it seasonably tells the school, “Blue is unavailable. These green folders are offered only as an accommodation; please decide whether to take them.” On those facts, the shipment does not constitute acceptance under G3. The notice changes the legal characterization. Further agreement may result from the school's response, but do not invent that response. Detailed rejection and remedy consequences belong to Contracts II.

The lesson is methodological: identify the communication accompanying conduct, not only the physical event. The same boxes can play a different contractual role because the seller has clearly described the proposal they carry.

## Read the forms rule in stages

The **[[battle of the forms]]** concerns exchanged documents containing nonmatching terms. Under G4, a definite and timely acceptance can operate despite an **[[additional term]]**, unless it is expressly conditional on assent to the new terms. An **[[expressly conditional acceptance]]** requires that condition; a document does not become conditional merely by printing standard terms on the back.

If acceptance forms the contract, analyze the additional term separately. With a nonmerchant involved, it is ordinarily a proposal requiring assent. Between merchants it may enter unless an exception applies, including an offer limiting acceptance to its terms, a **[[material alteration]]**, or a timely objection. Merchant status does not automatically incorporate every term. Whether a particular addition materially alters the deal is fact-sensitive; exercises may stipulate it so you can apply the rest of the rule.

A **[[different term]]** directly conflicts with an offered term. Courts vary on its treatment under subsection (2). Do not silently apply one jurisdiction's approach as a universal rule. If the writings do not form a contract but both parties act as though one exists, G4's conduct rule uses agreed written terms plus applicable statutory supplements. That is a distinct path, not proof that every term in the last form wins.

### Example 2: A timely acceptance with a dispute clause

A merchant buyer offers to buy 100 storage trays for 2,000 dollars and limits acceptance to its stated terms. The merchant seller promptly replies, “Accepted for 100 trays at 2,000 dollars,” adding a new arbitration clause. The reply is not expressly conditional. Assume the clause is a material alteration and the buyer never expressly assents to it.

First, the definite, timely and nonconditional acceptance supports formation under G4. Second, analyze the arbitration addition separately. The offer's limitation and the stipulated material alteration each block automatic entry through the between-merchants rule. The course facts support a contract without automatically incorporating that clause. Do not conclude either that all formation fails or that merchant silence accepts everything.

If the seller instead expressly conditions acceptance on the buyer's assent and the buyer does not assent, the writings may fail to create a contract. If they later ship and pay, analyze conduct under subsection (3). The terms would come from agreement plus applicable supplements; performance does not automatically accept the conditional arbitration demand. This course does not resolve independent arbitration-law issues or select a universal rule for conflicting terms.

## Build the Harbor analysis

Read the complete record before opening the model analysis. Harbor's transaction with Lumen involves services; its transaction with Paperline involves movable notebooks. Keep their communications and approvals separate. For Lumen, distinguish the conditional proposal, the narrower deposit reimbursement promise and the later signed service agreement. An April 8 writing can form a later bargain even if April 1 did not.

For Paperline, identify the order's quantity, signature and limited-terms language. Analyze the nonconditional acceptance and added arbitration clause. Then distinguish the formation conclusion from the delivery interpretation. The separate after-the-fact 100-dollar service bonus presents an existing-duty question; it does not retroactively eliminate the original service agreement.

Your assignment is a 900–1,200-word analysis using the record IDs and the course rule labels. Address both sides on disputed points, identify the best conclusion and specify what remains unresolved. Use short issue headings and paragraphs linking a rule to particular facts. Cite F, D, I and G labels as exercise authorities only. They are not real case citations.

## Self-assessment and revision

After drafting, compare your work with the model and rubric. Check whether you identified both agreements, preserved the board-approval qualification, analyzed reliance without automatic double recovery, screened writing requirements and distinguished a new form term from contract formation. Your memo should explain why the location phrase matters, not simply announce a delivery date.

Revise one overconfident sentence and one sentence that merely repeats a rule. Replace them with a fact-linked conclusion and a defined uncertainty. This course's quiz can test focused choices; it does not automatically grade the quality of your memo. The written work is self-assessed.

## Common mistakes

Avoid treating Article 2 as merchant-only law, every shipment as conforming acceptance, every extra form term as binding or every defect as destroying all agreements. Do not assume the last document controls merely because it came last.

## Key points

- Separate sales formation, included terms and performance.
- Apply each forms-rule stage and its exceptions.
- Analyze each Harbor promise independently before synthesizing.
- Use the record, counterarguments and qualified conclusions to support your memo.

banks.title: Contracts I: Formation and Interpretation questions

questions.stem: Under F1, a buyer purchases 80 ordinary movable desks, with no service component. Which framework applies?
choices: The common-law services framework because the desks support educational work.
The common-law framework unless the buyer also regularly sells desks.
The course Article 2 sales framework.
A mixed-transaction test solely because the desks must be delivered.
questions.explanation: F1 classifies movable desks as goods. Article 2 is not restricted to merchant-to-merchant transactions, and the buyer’s identity or the desks’ eventual location does not turn the sale into land or services.

questions.stem: A consultant offers a defined service for a fixed price. Her undisclosed diary says she hopes the recipient will decline. What matters most under F1?
choices: The commitment reasonably communicated by her words and conduct.
The consultant’s private intention, because outward assent requires matching hidden intent.
The recipient’s sincere belief, even if that belief conflicts with communicated terms.
The presence of a signature, because words and conduct cannot otherwise manifest assent.
questions.explanation: Objective assent examines communicated meaning in context. An undisclosed hope that the offer will be declined does not itself negate an otherwise serious offer; the recipient’s wish alone also cannot create one.

questions.stem: A buyer principally seeks reusable display panels. The manufacturer allocates 90% of the price to panels and 10% to layout help. Under the selected mixed-transaction test, what is the strongest analysis?
choices: Services predominate because any design assistance controls the classification.
Goods predominate solely because the larger price allocation mechanically settles the test.
Each component necessarily receives a separate governing rule under the selected test.
Goods likely predominate, considering purpose, business and allocation.
questions.explanation: The selected predominant-purpose test weighs several facts together. The buyer’s objective, supplier’s manufacturing business and large goods allocation support a goods classification; the percentage is relevant rather than mechanically conclusive.

questions.stem: Why must a real mixed-transaction dispute begin by checking the governing jurisdiction?
choices: A mixed sale requires proof of equal goods and service values before any framework applies.
Courts can use different classification approaches.
The supplier’s chosen document title conclusively selects the governing legal test.
The predominant-purpose test applies identically in every U.S. jurisdiction.
questions.explanation: F1 expressly selects a teaching test. Real jurisdictions may use different approaches, so the exercise’s classification method should not be presented as universal law.

questions.stem: A studio says, “Packages start around 900 dollars; send your scope and we will propose terms.” A customer replies, “Accepted.” What is the best F2 conclusion?
choices: The studio likely invited negotiation rather than supplied an offer.
The studio made an offer whose unresolved scope the customer may fill by accepting.
The starting price alone establishes a complete bargain despite the invitation to propose terms.
The customer’s reply confirms a contract and leaves the studio to choose its entire scope later.
questions.explanation: The starting price and request for scope leave the proposed exchange unsettled. The customer’s reply cannot create the present commitment missing from the studio’s communication.

questions.stem: Which message most clearly gives the recipient a present power to accept under F2?
choices: “I am considering selling this identified camera for 300 dollars; tell me if interested.”
“This camera’s price would be 300 dollars, subject to my committee’s final approval.”
“I offer this identified camera for 300 dollars; reply yes by noon.”
“I expect to offer this camera for 300 dollars after checking its condition.”
questions.explanation: The identified item, price and invited response communicate a present commitment. The alternatives describe possibilities, market information or a further approval process.

questions.stem: A detailed proposal says, “No contract until our director signs.” The recipient immediately says yes; the director has not signed. What is the best analysis?
choices: A detailed price and scope establish formation despite the express signature reservation.
The communicated signature reservation must be addressed before finding formation.
The recipient’s immediate assent supplies the missing director approval without more facts.
The reservation concerns only evidence of the contract and cannot affect when it forms.
questions.explanation: Definite terms do not erase an express reservation of commitment. The recipient’s assent does not, by itself, satisfy or remove the director-signature condition.

questions.stem: A learner says, “Advertisements can never be offers.” What correction best fits F2?
choices: An advertisement is an offer whenever it displays any price, despite remaining discretion.
An advertisement cannot be an offer because it addresses more than one potential customer.
An advertisement’s legal role depends on its heading rather than the commitment communicated.
Specific commitment and context can make an advertisement an offer.
questions.explanation: Advertisements usually invite offers, but the label does not decide every case. Specificity and communicated willingness to be bound can change the analysis; acceptance and other requirements still matter.

questions.stem: Match each communication to its best F1/F2 classification.
left: “We will consider your proposal.”
“Yes, I agree to your definite offer.”
A never-disclosed wish not to sell
“This specified desk for 70 dollars; your yes concludes the deal.”
choices: Preliminary negotiation
Manifestation of acceptance
Private intention
Offer
questions.explanation: The first leaves further decision open, the second communicates assent, the third is not communicated, and the fourth confers a power to conclude a defined bargain.

questions.stem: Under F1, the approach that evaluates reasonably communicated words and conduct is called ___ assent.
questions.explanation: Objective assent examines outward manifestations in context, rather than treating hidden intent alone as controlling.

questions.stem: Under F3, “I accept only if you add translation at no extra charge” is best classified as what?
choices: An acceptance because the original price is unchanged despite the added work condition.
A counteroffer because assent depends on a changed bargain.
A request because mentioning an extra term cannot qualify otherwise express assent.
An acceptance followed by a proposed modification, even though assent is expressly conditional.
questions.explanation: “Only if” makes assent conditional on new work. Under the common-law course rule, that is a counteroffer, unlike an unequivocal acceptance followed by a separate request.

questions.stem: Which reply most clearly accepts an editing offer while making a separate request?
choices: “I accept on the understanding that the editing price also covers layout.”
“I can accept once you confirm that layout is included in this offer.”
“I accept provided we reach an agreement about layout before work begins.”
“I accept the editing offer. Separately, what would layout cost?”
questions.explanation: The first sentence communicates present, unqualified assent. The second asks about a separate possibility without conditioning the acceptance on it.

questions.stem: An offer requires signed acceptance to be received by 4 p.m. Friday. It is posted Friday morning and arrives Monday. Under F3, what follows?
choices: Posting by Friday does not satisfy the express receipt deadline.
Posting by Friday satisfies the deadline because every authorized postal acceptance uses dispatch.
Signing by Friday satisfies the deadline even if the offeror receives the letter afterward.
The late arrival forms the contract because postal delay automatically extends a receipt deadline.
questions.explanation: An express receipt condition controls. The limited default dispatch rule does not displace it, and mailing does not itself create option protection.

questions.stem: A supplier sends an unsolicited proposal stating that silence will count as acceptance. There are no prior dealings or accepted benefits. Under F3, what is the best conclusion?
choices: Silence accepts because the offer explicitly tells the recipient how to reject it.
Silence accepts once the supplier waits a reasonable time, without any further conduct.
Silence alone ordinarily does not establish acceptance.
Silence accepts if the recipient had an opportunity to read the unsolicited proposal.
questions.explanation: The offeror cannot ordinarily impose contractual assent through silence alone. The problem supplies none of the circumstances that could support an exception.

questions.stem: An ordinary offer invites postal acceptance without a receipt condition. Revocation is mailed at 9 a.m.; acceptance is properly posted at 11 a.m.; revocation arrives next day. Under F3, when is acceptance effective?
choices: Never; the 9 a.m. revocation dispatch ends the power to accept before 11 a.m.
When the acceptance arrives, so the earlier-arriving revocation necessarily prevents formation.
When the offeror reads the acceptance, since authorized post only satisfies the method requirement.
At 11 a.m. when properly posted, before revocation is received.
questions.explanation: For this invited postal acceptance, dispatch is effective. Revocation generally requires receipt, so mailing revocation first does not terminate the power before the 11 a.m. acceptance.

questions.stem: A supported option requires acceptance by Friday and supplies no different timing rule. Acceptance is mailed Friday but received Monday. Under the course option rule, what is decisive?
choices: Friday dispatch is sufficient because option protection extends the ordinary mailbox rule.
Option acceptance is effective on receipt, making Monday too late.
Friday signing is sufficient because purchasing the option eliminates communication requirements.
Monday receipt is timely because mailing before Friday suspends the option’s expiry.
questions.explanation: F3 uses receipt for option acceptance. The separate option protection does not eliminate the deadline or convert the ordinary postal dispatch rule into an option rule.

questions.stem: An offer invites only completed fence painting by Sunday. The painter begins painting Friday; the owner then tries to revoke. Under F4, what is the best statement?
choices: Beginning the work forms an unconditional right to the entire price regardless of completion.
Buying brushes alone necessarily starts the protected invited performance on these facts.
Beginning the invited work protects the opportunity to complete, with payment still conditioned on completion.
The owner may revoke until completion because temporary protection requires a separate payment.
questions.explanation: F4 distinguishes preparation, actual beginning and completion. Beginning the requested painting creates temporary protection; it does not itself establish that the entire offered performance is complete.

questions.stem: An ordinary services offer says, “You may accept until Friday,” with no option consideration or other protection. What does that establish by itself?
choices: A lapse deadline, without necessarily preventing earlier effective revocation.
An irrevocable option, because a stated acceptance period itself supplies consideration.
An offer that requires acceptance to be received but needs no separate timing language.
A contract to perform the service, with Friday merely the deadline for confirming it.
questions.explanation: A stated deadline and irrevocability are different. F4 requires an independent basis for protection; a services offer is not made a goods firm offer merely by specifying Friday.

questions.stem: Match each event to the course timing concept.
left: Withdrawal reaches the offeree before acceptance
Proper invited postal acceptance of an ordinary offer is sent
Painter purchases ordinary brushes but has not begun the fence
Paid option acceptance reaches the offeror
choices: Effective ordinary revocation
Dispatch-based acceptance
Preparation
Receipt-based option acceptance
questions.explanation: F2–F4 distinguish receipt of revocation, limited postal dispatch, preparation and the receipt rule for options. The factual event must be matched to the applicable rule.

questions.stem: An independently supported promise to keep an offer open is an ___ contract.
questions.explanation: An option exchanges consideration for protection of the opportunity to accept. A deadline by itself is not necessarily an option.

questions.stem: Which fact most directly establishes consideration under F5?
choices: The report benefits the client, even though the promised fee was unrelated to obtaining it.
The consultant completes a report voluntarily before the client later promises payment in gratitude.
The client signs a payment promise without seeking any return promise or performance.
A promised report is sought in exchange for a promised fee.
questions.explanation: Consideration concerns what is sought and given in exchange. Usefulness, formality and gratitude alone do not establish that relationship.

questions.stem: A genuine sale exchanges a used table for 15 dollars despite its 200-dollar market value. Under F5, what is the best analysis?
choices: The exchange lacks consideration because the difference in market value is substantial.
The low price alone does not eliminate the actual bargain.
The low price makes the transaction a gift despite both parties intending a genuine exchange.
Consideration exists only if the seller can explain a commercially sensible reason for the discount.
questions.explanation: Adequacy differs from the existence of consideration. The problem supplies a genuine exchange; unequal price does not itself negate it or prove another defense.

questions.stem: “I am giving you my chair; collect it from my garage.” No service is sought from the recipient. What is the strongest F5 characterization?
choices: Collection is consideration because any effort required to receive property is a bargained service.
Collection necessarily converts the stated gift into a sale measured by the recipient’s travel cost.
Collection is likely a condition of receiving a gift.
The promise is a bargain because delivery conditions and requested exchange performances are equivalent.
questions.explanation: The stated purpose is delivery of a gift, not buying the recipient’s travel. Effort or inconvenience alone does not prove a bargained-for return.

questions.stem: A neighbor voluntarily returns a lost bag. Only afterward, without any earlier bargain, its owner promises 50 dollars in thanks. Under the basic F5 rule, what is missing?
choices: A return act bargained for in exchange for the later promise.
A monetary cost to the neighbor, because voluntarily returning property cannot involve legal effort.
A signature on the later promise, because every past-act promise fails only for lack of a writing.
An equal financial benefit to each party, because unequal benefits prevent a genuine exchange.
questions.explanation: The return preceded and was not induced as the requested exchange for the later promise. Gratitude and benefit do not by themselves supply the missing bargain; special exceptions are not supplied.

questions.stem: A buyer promises to purchase “whatever I choose, including nothing for any reason,” with no other restriction. What concern does F5 identify?
choices: The promise is a requirements commitment despite the explicit freedom to buy nothing for any reason.
The promise may be illusory because it preserves complete discretion.
The stated discretion supplies consideration because the buyer may voluntarily choose to perform.
The promise binds the buyer to a reasonable quantity even without any stated or implied constraint.
questions.explanation: The stated promise imposes no meaningful obligation. A genuine requirements commitment differs because a good-faith needs obligation can constrain discretion.

questions.stem: A translator demands 100 dollars more for the same work already owed to the same client. No exception or new duty is supplied. Under F6, what is the problem?
choices: The existing duty supplies no fresh consideration for the increase.
The original contract must be rescinded before either side may ever discuss a change.
The client’s agreement alone supplies fresh consideration even if no new obligation is undertaken.
The higher fee is supported because writing a new amount necessarily creates a new duty for the translator.
questions.explanation: The specified common-law rule requires more than doing the same existing duty. This concerns support for the change, not automatic destruction of the original agreement or a universal ban on increases.

questions.stem: The client adds five pages, and the translator agrees to translate them for an added fee. What distinguishes this from payment for unchanged work?
choices: The original pages cease to be owed as soon as additional pages are requested.
The higher fee alone supplies the translator’s new consideration, irrespective of added work.
A new promise to do the original work is sufficient even if the five pages are removed.
The translator undertakes a genuinely additional obligation.
questions.explanation: The new five-page duty can supply fresh consideration for the changed bargain. The original duty remains, and the services classification does not change merely because pages are involved.

questions.stem: For a goods modification under G5, which statement is correct?
choices: New consideration is unnecessary, so the seller’s announced price change alone establishes assent.
New consideration is unnecessary, so a modification cannot be challenged for an improper extraction.
