## Assignment and assumptions

Everything in this packet is original fiction. Dates are relative to the same fictional year; no weekday calculations are needed. Apply only the course F, D, I and G rules. The two transactions below are separate. All participants are adults with capacity, authorized to speak for their businesses. No facts support illegality, misrepresentation, duress or unconscionability unless a later exercise expressly changes them. The typed signatures in R5–R7 were deliberately adopted and satisfy the exercise's electronic-record requirements. Monetary amounts are U.S. dollars.

Write a 900–1,200-word analysis of whether enforceable agreements exist, what supports them, which added terms enter, and the meaning of the delivery commitment. Include the reliance alternative, the bonus and the writing screen. Discuss counterarguments and remaining limits. Do not calculate final breach damages or bar eligibility. The writing task is self-assessed; it is not automatically scored by the quiz.

## Services: Harbor and Lumen

### R1 — April 1 proposal

Lumen, a communications consultancy, sends Harbor this message:

> We propose a workshop plan and a two-hour rehearsal for 1,800 dollars, due May 20. No workshop contract exists until Harbor's board approves and both sides sign a service agreement.

The scope is communications planning and rehearsal; no sale of goods is involved. Harbor's coordinator replies, “This sounds good. I will take it to the board.” The board has not yet approved.

### R2 — April 2 reimbursement promise

The same authorized Harbor coordinator writes:

> Please reserve the rehearsal room today so we do not lose it. If the board declines the workshop, Harbor will reimburse the nonrefundable room deposit up to 300 dollars. This promise does not approve the full workshop.

### R3 — April 2 payment and causation

After reading R2, Lumen pays a nonrefundable 240-dollar room deposit. The receipt identifies the rehearsal room and May 18 booking. Lumen would not have booked without R2. Harbor anticipated the booking when it sent the message. No refund, credit or other use of this deposit is available. Lumen also claims 700 dollars for a reusable tablet bought March 25 for its general consulting work, before R1 or R2.

### R4 — April 5 board decision

The board approves proceeding with the workshop. Harbor reports the approval but says the signature requirement in R1 remains. No signed service agreement yet exists. The actual record therefore does not trigger R2's express board-decline condition. A separate practice variation asks what would happen if the board declined; keep that variation distinct from the actual facts.

### R5 — April 8 signed service agreement

Harbor and Lumen both sign electronically:

> Lumen will deliver the workshop plan and provide the two-hour rehearsal by May 20 for 1,800 dollars. The 240-dollar room cost is included in that price. This is the complete and final agreement for the workshop project, including room costs; it replaces earlier negotiations about those project terms. Harbor will pay on completion.

The parties deliberately adopt R5 as a complete integration of these project terms. The document makes no promise to pay the tablet expense. There is no qualifying defense to the parties' assent. These services can be completed within one year of April 8.

### R6 — April 12 proposed bonus

Lumen asks for an additional 100 dollars for the same plan and rehearsal, explaining only that it would prefer a higher fee. Harbor replies with an adopted electronic signature, “Agreed, 100 dollars extra.” Lumen undertakes no new duty, gives up no disputed claim and identifies no unanticipated circumstance. Apply F6's basic common-law existing-duty rule; no statutory or other exception is supplied. No new reliance on the bonus is established.

## Goods: Harbor and Paperline

### R7 — April 10 notebook order

Harbor sends Paperline a signed purchase order:

> 200 custom notebooks, 2,000 dollars total, with the attached Harbor cover design. Delivery to Harbor's workshop address by June 14 for distribution at the June 15 workshop. Acceptance is limited to the terms of this order.

Harbor's full street address is included. The goods are movable notebooks; design printing is incidental. Both parties are merchants for the relevant Article 2 rules. The order's quantity and signatures meet D5 and D6. There is no unilateral cancellation clause. The order does not invite acceptance only by completed performance.

### R8 — April 11 response

Paperline promptly responds:

> Accepted: 200 notebooks, 2,000 dollars, delivery to Harbor by June 14, using the attached cover design. Our standard terms also require arbitration of all disputes.

The response is a definite, timely acceptance and is not expressly conditional on Harbor's assent to arbitration. For this exercise, the new arbitration clause materially alters the bargain. Harbor never expressly assents to it. No other exchanged form contains an arbitration term. Do not infer that all arbitration clauses are material alterations in every real transaction from this stipulated fact.

### R9 — Earlier discussion and final delivery term

On April 9, before R7 and R8, Paperline mentioned, “We usually send workshop orders out the day before the event.” Harbor did not agree to a dispatch-only obligation. The parties adopt the matching delivery language in R7 and R8 as a final expression of that term. There is no established course of dealing between them, no qualifying trade usage and no course of performance changing that term. Paperline later says it plans to hand the boxes to a carrier on June 14 for arrival June 16. No such shipment has yet occurred.

### R10 — Boundaries of the record

No notebook shipment, payment, in-court admission or substantial manufacturing beginning has occurred. None is needed to invent a writing exception when the signed record already satisfies the stated writing rule. No later modification of delivery is agreed. The record does not establish a completed breach, damages, mitigation or the procedure for demanding assurance. Those performance questions are reserved for Contracts II.

## Drafting checklist

1. Classify each transaction and explain why.
2. Analyze the service approval and signature sequence.
3. Distinguish the deposit promise, the actual approval and the board-decline variation.
4. Identify consideration for R5 and the issue with R6.
5. Apply the goods formation and additional-terms rules separately.
6. Screen each agreement for writing requirements.
7. Compare arrival and dispatch interpretations using R7–R9.
8. State limits without inventing extra facts or duplicating recovery.

references.title: Exercise rules: interpretation and sales formation
references.body:
## Interpretation rules

I1. Read the whole agreement before isolating a word. State competing plausible meanings and connect each to text, transaction purpose and permissible context. An undisclosed private definition is weak evidence of shared meaning. If parties attach materially different reasonable meanings and neither has reason to know the other's, the course rule may yield no agreement on that term; knowledge can change whose meaning controls. Not every disagreement is a failure of assent.

I2. An integration is a writing adopted as final for the terms it contains. A partial integration bars contradictory prior or contemporaneous terms but can permit consistent additions. A complete integration also excludes consistent additional prior or contemporaneous terms within its scope. An integration clause is evidence, not a magic eraser of fraud or every contextual issue. Interpretation, validity challenges and later modifications are distinct from adding an earlier inconsistent promise. Jurisdictions disagree about when context may be consulted and how clauses affect the inquiry; questions specify the course approach.

I3. In the course goods problems, course of performance means conduct under this agreement with repeated opportunities and knowledge/acquiescence; course of dealing concerns earlier transactions between these parties; usage of trade concerns a sufficiently established practice in the relevant trade. Seek a consistent reading. When irreconcilable under the selected Article 1 hierarchy, express terms prevail over performance, performance over dealing, and dealing over usage. Qualification, reasonable notice and waiver questions can matter. Do not invent a trade practice from a single witness's preference.

## Sales rules

G1. Article 2 concerns sales of goods, not only deals between merchants. Agreement may appear through words or conduct; the exact moment can be uncertain. Open terms do not necessarily defeat formation when intent to contract and a sufficiently certain basis for a remedy remain. This does not supply an unlimited missing quantity; requirements/output contracts need their own good-faith framework. These lessons do not decide software, digital assets, international sales or specialized consumer statutes.

G2. A merchant's signed assurance to keep a goods offer open can be irrevocable without option consideration for the stated period or a reasonable period, capped at three months under the firm-offer provision. If the offeree supplied the form, the assurance must be separately signed by the offeror. A six-month assurance is not automatically six months of statutory irrevocability; a supported option may protect a longer period independently. Expiration of firm-offer protection is not necessarily expiration of the offer itself.

G3. Unless language or circumstances unambiguously indicate otherwise, a goods offer invites a reasonable manner and medium of acceptance. An order for prompt shipment may be accepted by a prompt promise to ship or by shipment. A nonconforming shipment can both accept and breach; seasonable notice that it is only an accommodation prevents that shipment from being an acceptance under this rule. Missing reasonable notice of beginning a requested performance may permit the offeror to treat the offer as lapsed.

G4. Under the selected 2-207 framework, a definite, timely acceptance can form a contract despite additional or different terms unless expressly conditional on assent to them. Additional terms are proposals; between merchants they may enter unless the offer limits acceptance to its terms, the addition materially alters the bargain, or a timely objection applies. Silence does not automatically accept a material addition. Courts differ on treatment of different, conflicting terms; this course does not assume one universal outcome under subsection (2). If the writings fail to form a contract but both parties' conduct recognizes one, subsection (3) uses agreed written terms plus applicable statutory supplements. Continuing performance is not automatically assent to every conditional-form term.

G5. A goods modification requires no new consideration, but good faith and applicable statute-of-frauds and signed-modification requirements remain. A defective modification can raise waiver questions; waiver and retraction are reserved for Contracts II.

## Primary-text comparisons

- [UCC 2-204](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-204), [2-205](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-205), [2-206](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-206) and [2-207](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-207): formation, firm offers, shipment and forms.
- [UCC 2-202](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-202) and [Washington's enacted 62A.2-202](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=62A.2-202): final writings and context; note updated cross-references in the enactment.
- [UCC 2-209](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-209) and [1-304](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/1/1-304): modification and good faith.
- [Washington 62A.1-303](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=62A.1-303): contextual categories and hierarchy as an illustrative enacted source.

These are reading anchors, not substitutes for checking controlling enacted law.

For contrasting interpretation questions, read [Masterson v. Sine, 68 Cal. 2d 222, 225–27 (1968)](https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/masterson-v-sine-32881/) on whether a writing is a complete integration, and [Joyner v. Adams, 87 N.C. App. 570, 575–76 (1987)](https://madisonian.net/downloads/contracts/joyner.pdf) on differing meanings and knowledge. These are historical state opinions, not a uniform modern rule for every jurisdiction.
